source.title: Sparse Autoencoders Work on Attention Layer Outputs

page_placements.theme: SAE latent monosemanticity depends on activation range, scoring metric and evaluation harness

record.tranche_reason: The study tests how SAE-feature interpretations vary with activation range using feature-to-proxy comparisons, rather than measuring individual-neuron polysemanticity with the original method.
record.gate_note: The results concern SAE features learned from attention-layer outputs and an attention head, not individual vision neurons or MLP neurons. The study explicitly reports that feature specificity is higher in upper activation ranges and that lower ranges contain more polysemanticity. SAE training statistics, induction-feature counts, and unrelated upstream-circuit analyses are not recorded as claim-version rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains a sparse autoencoder on attention-layer outputs of gelu-2l and reports on SAE features and one attention head. It never measures individual neurons in vision or language models. V7 concerns whether a neuron counts as polysemantic depending on activation range. The study's finding that lower ranges hold more polysemanticity is about learned SAE features, a different unit. The authors cite Bricken et al. for the neuron-level analogue rather than testing it. The SAE method assumes superposition and uses it as a tool without testing it. The related findings are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that SAEs trained on attention outputs learn sparse, interpretable features: about 82% of the 76% non-dead features in a sample of 50. Their features retain nontrivial polysemanticity, especially at lower activation ranges, which they expect wider SAEs and better training to reduce. They also present L1H6 as an example of attention-head polysemanticity, and suggest attention SAEs could help study attention head superposition.
record.recipe_differences: The post says it replicates the Anthropic MLP SAE approach, but trains on concatenated attention-head z vectors from the final layer of a two-layer language model rather than MLP activations.
record.method_sensitivity: Interpretation specificity varies with feature activation range: the authors report higher specificity in upper ranges and more false positives or polysemanticity in lower ranges.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE features on gelu-2l attention outputs are highly specific to their proxy contexts in upper activation ranges but show false positives or polysemanticity in lower ranges. Source-token variance explained rises with the activation threshold, reaching over 99.9% at threshold 5 for the board feature.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Whether an SAE feature appears monosemantic depends on which part of its activation range is examined; low activations are more polysemantic.

fits_no_version.finding: Mean-ablating induction head L1H6 turns off 98.44% of induction features and raises loss on three non-induction code features (+0.11, +0.30, +0.51). Ablating control head L1H0 has smaller or negligible effects.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Individual attention heads are polysemantic, serving induction and unrelated code-completion roles.

record.problems: The post calls its proxy masks crude or suboptimal and reports a 0.50 correlation for the board feature. It notes potential false positives and false negatives, and says the induction-feature automation may have false positives and false negatives. This is a small, selected investigation of SAE features in one two-layer model, not a systematic study of individual neurons.

untested.parts: No vision models or image-classifier neurons.
No MLP neurons measured. The study uses SAE features on attention outputs of one two-layer model.
Superposition is assumed by the SAE method, not tested as the cause of neuron polysemanticity.
No tests of initialization, regularization or training noise.
No comparison of activation functions, architectures or regularization.
Canonical polysemantic neurons are not revisited.
No neuron-level analysis of activation range or explanation scoring. The activation-range results apply to SAE features only.

record.verdict_notes: This is a two-week MATS sprint on one SAE for one two-layer model. The reader's V7 link conflates SAE features with neurons, and the versions are all phrased about neurons. If the phenomenon file is later widened to cover dictionary features or attention heads, rows r1-r7 could be relinked to a feature-level analogue of V7 and r8-r13 to head polysemanticity.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses a language model, not an image classifier, and does not test vision neurons.
It studies SAE features on attention-layer outputs, not a large share of MLP neurons in transformer language models.
The authors speculate that a too-small SAE may leave features unrecovered, but do not test whether superposition causes polysemanticity.
The study does not test initialization, regularization, or training noise as causes of polysemanticity under sufficient capacity.
There is no comparison of activation functions, architectures, or regularization, nor a test of lowering polysemanticity while preserving performance.
The study does not revisit canonical neurons to establish that their unrelated activations share one feature.
The study examines activation ranges and proxy-based interpretation for selected SAE features, but does not systematically compare explanation-scoring methods or classify neurons.

relation.reason: It applies the SAE method to attention outputs and measures no neurons.

tranche.reason: The study uses SAEs on concatenated attention z vectors (layer 1 of gelu-2l) as a tool. Its polysemanticity findings concern SAE features and attention head L1H6, not neurons, so it tests no version.

source_check.notes: All findings concern SAE features on the final-layer attention outputs (concatenated hook_z) of gelu-2l, or the polysemanticity of attention head L1H6. None concern neurons. Rows link to no version. The 99.9% figure is for feature 14 at threshold 5. The pet feature's specificity has no activation-range split.

statements.correction: Board feature (14): 'board' source tokens explain over 99.9% of head 1.6 DFA variance at activation threshold 5. The share rises with the threshold. The pet feature's share also rises with higher activations, but the text gives no number. Upper-range specificity with lower-range false positives or polysemanticity is shown for features 14 and 99. These are SAE features, not neurons.
statements.problem: Nothing material. 'Over 99%' is a looser form of the text's 'over 99.9%', which is reported for the board feature (feature 14, head 1.6) at threshold 5. The upper/lower range split is shown for features 14 and 99, and the Limitations section says it holds for SAE features in general.
